newsitem.title: UK: Mark firms on EMU nervousness, Buba rate worries.
newsitem.headline: Mark firms on EMU nervousness, Buba rate worries.

text.p: The mark firmed on the crosses in Europe's morning, helped by renewed worries over monetary union and vague speculation that the Bundesbank might switch to a variable rate repo tender after its council meeting today.

Nervousness regarding Germany's budget deficit and the country's ability to meet the three-percent deficit-to-GDP was heightened ahead of the presentation of Bonn's 1997 supplementary and 1998 budget proposals on Friday, traders said.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel's draft budget foresees the federal deficit at 71.2 billion marks this year and 57.8 billion in 1998, according to documents obtained by Reuters.
Also, French daily La Tribune reported on Thursday that an audit of French public finances, due on July 21, is likely to show a 1997 deficit of 3.6 to 3.7 percent of GDP.
Although an overshoot of that size was expected by the market, traders said it was not helping matters today.

"There were worries that the Germans won't accept the French budget deficit... Still, it's not such a large move (in mark/Paris). The interest in mark/Paris has been so low, it just looks like a big move," said one trader at a Belgian bank here.
The mark was at 3.3813/18 French francs at 0910 GMT, just off its earlier highs, and up from 3.3741/46 in late Europe on Thursday.

Traders said a slide in Italian and French government bonds this morning was also giving the mark a boost on the European crosses, despite the mark's fall to a new 41-month low against the dollar and a 23-month low against the yen earlier.
Mark/lira was at 977.15/45 against 974.10/60 on Wednesday.
Meanwhile, the market was also awaiting the Bundesbank's news conference at 1015 GMT -- traditionally held after the central bank's one council meeting per year outside Frankfurt.
Traders were not expecting a change in the discount or Lombard rates, but there was speculation over the repo rate.

"If they do (make it a variable rate), it could be seen as a sign from the German authorities to add some uncertainty over rates and perhaps help bring down the dollar/mark," said the Belgian bank trader.
"They wouldn't have to actually hike rates if they make it a variable repo and leave it open."
Analysts said the idea of switching to a variable repo rate was somewhat far-fetched, adding that it was likely to be an opportunity to take profits.
"People have been very short in the mark on the crosses for quite some time, and such rumours would be a good excuse (to buy marks)," said Ernesto Ramirez, European economist at Bankers Trust.
"After the Bundesbank news conference today, we'll probably get an easing of this upward pressure on the mark," said Ramirez.
However, they also said it was understandable that such speculation should unnerve the market as it would raise the spectre of higher German interest rates in the not so far off future.
"I don't believe they will... but if they were to float, people would perceive it as a sign that the interest rate cycle had turned," said Glenn Davies, chief economist at Credit Lyonnais Laing.
This would put the French authorities in a bit of a quandary as they were loath to see higher rates, Davies added.
"The market will be a little less confident that rates in Germany won't go up at all for a period of time...there is a little change in sentiment there," Bankers Trust's Ramirez said.
-- Chizu Nomiyama, London Forex Desk, +44-171-542-6721
